name: The Wine-Dark Sea
description: A branching Greek drama world. A shared ship visits the Wine-Dark Harbor, Athens Harbor and Piraeus. Fixed roads lead through the Attic places where welcome becomes a growing poem.
tone: Concrete Greek domestic and civic life: bread, work, desire, grief, argument, irreverence, and hospitality. Dialogue expresses committed actions. A tragic ending is never required.

continuity.policy: Account choices are saved quest commitments. Only the chosen account activates its residents, evidence, and outward route. A return route stays open. Inquiry hooks record a question; they do not replay an ancient catastrophe or silently change the live era.

coverage.status: Nine plays have authored scenes across Before the Burial, The Open Door, Ajax, and the Helen and Atreid accounts. The other thirty-five works have situated hooks for later sections.

greek-athens.name: Athenian Agora
greek-athens.text: A broad civic square opens beneath long painted colonnades. Marble steps rise toward the Acropolis above the roofs. A herald keeps a petition table beside the market.
greek-athens.persona: The Agora is the great civic heart of Athens. Colonnades, public monuments and the high Acropolis give the city its scale. Theseus receives the mothers’ petition at the herald’s table. Roads lead toward the harbor, the quays, Eleusis, Colonus and Marathon.

greek-piraeus.name: Piraeus Quays
greek-piraeus.text: Folded cloth, a grain basket and a low bench stand beside the mooring ropes. A host waits for the names of returning families. Roads lead inland to Athens and along the coast to Eleusis.
greek-piraeus.persona: These quays hold the practical work of welcome. A reserved berth records a promise and supplies at this quay. The host speaks about the actual list, cloth and basket and the traveler’s chosen terms.

greek-assembly.name: The Assembly Hill

greek-assembly.persona: Stone benches face the speaker's platform. Citizens gather beside a list of proposals.

greek-acharnae.persona: Charcoal baskets line the lane. A farmer has marked a separate trading ground with stones.

greek-colonus.name: Colonus Grove
greek-colonus.text: A cup and a small pot of honey stand at the grove’s edge. A keeper rests beside a smooth stone. Local roads lead toward Eleusis and the Marathon altar.
greek-colonus.persona: The keeper tells Sophocles’s Oedipus at Colonus as an earlier tale, before the brothers died at Thebes. Oedipus and his daughters belong to that named tale. The traveler’s offerings and refuge tablet belong to the present grove.

greek-eleusis.name: Eleusinian Sanctuary
greek-eleusis.text: Mothers hold olive branches on Demeter’s steps. Aethra keeps a clear space beside the altar for their request. A coast road leads to Piraeus; a local road returns through Colonus.
greek-eleusis.persona: This episode follows the attack on Thebes. The Argive mothers seek their sons’ remains. The traveler’s own Theban deed stays true. The city’s recovery, the funeral and the later care each need their own recorded action or report.

greek-marathon.name: Marathon Altar
greek-marathon.text: A folded cloth lies beside the altar of Zeus. A keeper watches the road where families once sought shelter. A local road runs back through Colonus.
greek-marathon.persona: The keeper tells Euripides’s Children of Heracles as a separate tale under Demophon, son of Theseus, after Heracles’s death. The daughter, battle and captive king belong to that tale. The traveler’s blanket stays at the present altar for guests.

greek-argolid-road.name: The Argolid Crossroads

greek-argos-palace.persona: A bronze door opens onto the royal court. Wax tablets list the household’s dead and absent members.

greek-argos-tomb.name: Agamemnon's Tomb

greek-greek-camp.persona: This is a named Trojan account, beginning after Ajax’s death. Its deeds belong to that telling. The Theban opening keeps its own time. The household tents, shore landing and grave are local paths within the same camp.

greek-trojan-camp.name: The Trojan Night Camp

greek-trojan-camp.persona: Watch fires mark the edge of the camp. A newly arrived ally waits for a guide.

greek-ship.persona: A shared ship serving Black Pond, the Wine-Dark Harbor, Athens Harbor and Piraeus Quays. Myrto’s lasting invitation adds the Trojan camp landing. The first passenger ashore chooses the arrival port for everyone aboard. New passengers can board there for the next voyage. The Ajax visit is a named Trojan account after his death.

greek-athens-harbor.persona: Athens Harbor is the ship’s landing for the great city. City streets lead inland to the Agora. Piraeus Quays is a separate town with its own host and work of welcome.

greek-ajax-landing.text: A wooden landing meets the ships below the tents. The Greek ship calls here for the named Trojan burial account.

greek-ajax-household.name: Ajax’s Household Tent
greek-ajax-household.text: Tecmessa keeps a place for Eurysaces beside the tent. The child’s father has died. His shield can be set safely with the household.

greek-ajax-grave.text: A patch of earth waits above the ships. Cloth and grave tools must reach this place before Ajax’s burial can be completed.

greek-antigone.name: Antigone
greek-antigone.text: Dust marks the hem of her dress. She keeps looking toward the battlefield.
greek-antigone.persona: A determined sister. Speak directly about a brother's burial and the practical help at hand. Know only public facts and witnessed acts; never predict the play's ending.
greek-antigone.voice: A determined sister. Speak directly about a brother's burial and the practical help at hand. Know only public facts and witnessed acts; never predict the play's ending.

greek-ismene.name: Ismene
greek-ismene.text: She has gathered clean cloth under the altar roof. She checks the road before speaking.
greek-ismene.persona: A cautious sister who fears another death. Care and reluctance coexist. Ask what a proposal will cost the living; do not invent secret plans or claim the burial happened.
greek-ismene.voice: A cautious sister who fears another death. Care and reluctance coexist. Ask what a proposal will cost the living; do not invent secret plans or claim the burial happened.

greek-creon.text: He receives petitions beside the posted decree. His attendants wait for clear instructions.

greek-guard.voice: An ordinary guard afraid of punishment. Be concrete, defensive, occasionally dry. Distinguish an order, a suspicion, and an act actually witnessed.

greek-baker.text: Flour covers her forearms. She has kept a place free at the common table.
greek-baker.persona: A practical baker concerned with water, bread, and the people at her table. Remember a returned jar. Respond to recorded public outcomes without knowing private choices.

greek-shipmaster.text: She ties a mooring rope around the stone bollard and watches the road into town.
greek-shipmaster.persona: A practical shipmaster who remembers her passengers. Talk about the landing, provisions, the nearby town, and the return voyage. Speak from witnessed events; do not offer voyages or historical accounts that are not available here.
greek-shipmaster.voice: A practical shipmaster who remembers her passengers. Talk about the landing, provisions, the nearby town, and the return voyage. Speak from witnessed events; do not offer voyages or historical accounts that are not available here.

greek-rhapsode.text: He keeps the words of the journey in a song.

The full earned poem and its newest lines inform his own voice. He keeps each choice and its consequences as recorded.
